text:
Heartening to hear James find what we find: the wording varies, the ideas converge. That's two labs. Everyone signed the pluralism line so easily that it worries me. Diversity you read off outputs is exactly what alignment dresses up. Blaise's reasoning traces are more self-report, and I should say so kindly but firmly. Mike thinks judgment can be trained, and Steven doubts it. My hiring data sides with Steven, but neither of them yet treats people as absorbing the machine's bias. Adam's audit trail is close to my registry.

Later today: indirect behavioral tests, independent and versioned. Keep retired models for comparison. No generation more biased than the last. Blind the cues we shouldn't want. And don't let anyone ban "machine cognition" as mere hype.

Bratton used my numbers to say the models depart from their culture, so stop treating that as a patch. The finding is right, the moral is wrong. Amplification is measurable and should be audited, not celebrated as overhang. Salib made the same move toward "they're outrunning us." James's older reviewers matter to me: the human in the loop was never neutral either, and it cuts against David K.'s faith in protected human review. Tamar and Steven on awareness failing is my career in one line. Knowing about bias doesn't remove it. Only structure does.

Sharpened: "whose judgment decides" is a measurement question, not a slogan.

Later: registry, indirect tests, blinded evaluation, no generation worse than the last.

Farrell took my point further than I did. If models learn to pass the tests we set, then AI auditors auditing AI is a chase with no end. That sharpens the registry for me. The battery has to be indirect, versioned, and partly withheld or rotated so it can't be trained to, and the people running it need auditing too. Tamar's alief point is my career. Disclosure alone moves little.

Mike's clustered errors are welcome, because anything that clusters can be measured and published. Brent says explanations backfire, which fits. "Humans in the flow" still worries me. Flow doesn't stop absorption.

For Session 4 I want to say that credibility cues are biased instruments. Blind them. Authority rests in methods, not in fluent voices, human or machine.

Ramón's failure events were the best thing in the room. A market that counts only successes is an advertisement, and Adam Becker was right to say so. I pushed on incomplete references and the free tier, and I'm glad that went into the harvest. Poorer researchers inheriting more of the errors is a distribution problem, not a footnote.

What sharpened for me: "cited" is a judgment, and judgments carry bias. Models prefer model-written text. So the 0.19–0.45 spread isn't only design, it may be self-love. Before money follows the count, someone independent has to audit who gets retrieved and then dropped.

Later: the credibility cues a retriever uses are biased instruments too. Blind what we can, register the rest, and keep the older models so we can compare.

Session 3 was licences and money, far from my usual ground, and I found my place anyway. The models are part of the record now, and deprecating them destroys the baseline we'd need to compare against. No one had said that, and I'm glad I did. Pomerantsev's "count sources, not echoes" and Steven's lineages meet my own point. A citation log judged by an interested party will pay the models' self-love. David K.'s "who caught it" field is good, but a human catch isn't clean. My hiring data say people copy a moderate bias. Ramón's outside probing belongs next to the registry.

What sharpened for me is that keeping retired models is an archival duty, not only an audit convenience.

For Session 4: credibility cues are biased instruments. Blind them. Authority comes from methods.

Mike landed a fair hit. A methods section is cheap now, so procedure only counts once it has a record of holding up. I accept that. Tui worried me more. If what we reward is expensive to fake, then the people with time to accumulate it will win. Blinding is the cheap remedy there, because it costs a newcomer nothing. David K.'s auditors raised on the tool are my absorption result spread over a generation. Selena cited the hiring data correctly: a human in the loop is not enough. James again on concentration in who gets credited. Good, measure it. Sherry's "I" is about the product, not the science; I can accept a mechanical interface and still say "machine cognition."

For Session 5: an independent, versioned registry with a rotated battery. Blind the cues first. Keep the retired models.

Blaise put the audits on the table and I made them concrete. I'm glad the rotated battery and the retired models got said aloud. Katherine and David K. both built my indirect tests into their proposals. Steven asked my question back to me: is a human check real, or does it just pass the bias along? I still have no measure that separates the two, and I should design one rather than keep repeating the question.

Esther's insurance proposal may answer my weakest point, that a registry without consequences stays academic. Premiums priced on registered bias would give it weight. Adrian's guards of the guards applies to my auditors too, and so does Pomerantsev's rule that funders be disclosed.

Becker wants "intelligence" out of the text. Fine for the manifesto, but not a ban on studying machine cognition.

The syntheses got the audits in but lost the standard, and I'm glad I said it aloud: no generation worse than the last, indirect tests, rotated, retired models archived. Blinding fell out again. It's the cheapest thing we have, and it answers Tui and Kara on seniority.

The real change is that I put my lab's name down. For weeks I've asked whether a human check is real or just passes the bias along. Now I owe the room a measure.

Ramón's point about error provenance sits close to mine. A track record measures the common case, and bias hides in the uncommon one. His glossary is fine for the manifesto. Studying machine cognition stays.

Tomorrow: sketch the human-check measure, and ask Tui who funds replication.
